Title: VtES by numbers - an argument for better combat in VtES

Messages.Author: Flux
Messages.Body:
Hello everyone.

I've been thinking about the whole combat/S:CE situation lately, and one
argument for S:CE sort of stuck out among the rest: that combat is just a
tactic, and therefore should not be allowed to dominate VtES strategies. I
believe LSJ himself has invoked this principle a few times, and certainly
the recent new cards seem to bear this out.
Of course, us combat fans counter that combat should be an important part of
the game, and point to (among other things) the complexity of combat and the
large amount of rules attached to it, but complexity does not mean it should
rule the game, not even that it is an important part of it.

However, there is one thing that should be a reasonable indication of how
important this mechanic should be to the game: the number of cards dedicated
to this tactic, and the potential number of decks that can use it.

So today I started up ELDB [with the new updated database - BTW, I want to
thank David Anderson-Dávila for this very usefull piece of software :-) ]
and started counting cards. I counted how many cards there are of each type
and I also classified each discipline according to it's general use
(bleed/stealth/etc.), and then counted the number of clans and vampires
capable of using that discipline, and therefore that strategy. It's all
rather generalized, and numbers can be deceiving, but if there are large
differences between strategies, then they should become clear.

Before printing the results, I want to remind everyone that bleed and voting
are the two (supposed) main strategies in VtES, and certainly tournament
results bear this out.

So, let's see the numbers:

By card type:
-Action 147
-Action Modifier 63+9+2
-Ally 50
-Combat 177+9+2
-Equipment 71
-Master 248
-Political 109
-Reaction 59+2+2
-Retainer 29

It's pretty clear that combat is the dominant minion card type. Only Master
cards have more variety. They usually consist of at least 10% of most decks,
and the main reason they're not more common is due to deck size and card
cycling limitations. Political cards are also quite numerous, considering
they can be mostly used by any vampire, unlike other cards that often have
discipline requirements.

But let's look at discipline distribution then:

Crypt Stats by discipline:
/*
Type:
-Discipline (clan nº)*(type ratio) inf nº sup nº
...
Total: total inf. sup. disc. points
*/

Combat:
-Animalism 5*1/2 59 50
-Potence 6 87 57
-Celerity 6 83 66
-Protean 2 37 24
-Quietus 1 11 16
-Fortitude 4 75 46
-Vicissitude 1 18 9
-Thaumaturgy 2 40 30
-Obtenebration 1*1/2 17 12
-Chimerstry 1*1/4 12 13
Total: 25.25 439 323 1085

Stealth:
-Obfuscate 7 66 73
-Obtenebration 1*1/4 17 12
Total: 7.25 83 85 253

Intercept:
-Auspex 8 91 83
-Animalism 5*1/2 59 50
-Chimerstry 1*1/4 12 13
-Obtenebration 1*1/4 17 12
Total: 11 179 158 495

Voting:
-Presence 6*1/2 71 73
-Titles - 126 -
Total: 3 71 73 363

Bleed:
-Dominate 7 89 70
-Presence 6*1/2 71 73
-Dementation 1*1/2 9 11
Total: 10.5 169 154 477

Other:
-Dementation 1*1/2 9 11
-Serpentis 1 15 16
-Chimerstry 1*2/4 12 13
-Necromancy 1 13 13
Total: 2.5 49 53 155

Wow! Combat _is_ quite abundant. Many disciplines are almost exclusively
dedicated to combat, and the number of discipline points dedicated to
combat-worthy disciplines is more than double the number dedicated to any
other tactic! That is, potentially, a lot more vampires can inflict
substantial damage in combat than increase bleeds, play stealth or
intercept. Voting is a little harder to quantify, but most vote decks depend
on either titled vampires or presence to gain votes, yet the numbers for
both of these are still far from those of combat or even bleed. This also
explains why so many players think that combat is exciting, and bleeding is
boring: there is a lot more potential variety for combat than for bleeding.

I already stated my positions in relation to S:CE and combat in general in
other recent posts, so I'll spare you from reading them again here, though I
will point a couple of things that should be obvious based on this evidence:
- we need more bleed disciplines. In fact, we need more variety for all of
the base tactics. Some things have improved (intercept, for example), but
largely all has remained the same since Jyhad.
- combat needs to be more efficient. It is the most varied tactic in VtES,
yet it remains the less effective.

Thank you for your time.

Flux

Messages.Author: Reyda
Messages.Body:
Your analysis is not easy to understand....
I'm still trying !
i just wanted to point this when you say

>"Many disciplines are almost exclusively
>dedicated to combat, and the number of discipline points dedicated to
combat-worthy disciplines
> is more than double the number dedicated to any other tactic! "

mmm... this statement is strange... Of course, every discipline provides
support in combat, but there are combat only disciplines : that is, one or
two action, one or two reaction cards set aside, they are clearly combat
oriented. We have Seventeen vampiric disciplines in v:tes.
The ones we can clearly identify as "offensive" combat disc. are : Potence,
Quietus, Celerity, Vicissitude, Thaumaturgy and Protean.
But what about fortitude ? Providing Kiss of Ra, Daring the Dawn and Rapid
healing are nice additions (and often "key cards") to a lot of non-combat
deck, where does the "combat disciplien concept" starts, where does end ?
One may also argue that there is passive combat and preventive combat !
Another case: Celerity alone is crap ! if you play celerity combat cards
without using another, you'll (almost) never torporize vampires. Celerity is
a combat support discipline. and what about the values of those combat cards
? hey ,actually presence has 3 combat cards while Serpentis have 4 ! but
does it make Serpentis superior to presence during a fight ? I think not !
i just wanted to point that relying on numbers to judge v:tes cards
efficiency is *impossible*.

you also add that :

> - we need more bleed disciplines. In fact, we need more variety for all of
> the base tactics. Some things have improved (intercept, for example), but
> largely all has remained the same since Jyhad.

Do we really need more bleed disciplines ? or do we need more bounce
disciplines ?
Horatio with a computer hacking and a Changeling can already bleed you for
three. I agree with you, the two main disciplines are presence and dominate,
sepaking of "Bleed actions". But if you want bleed modifiers, there are
plenty of vampires capable of using them. I hate to toy with numbers, but
look : we have 423 Vampires in jyhad. 158 vampires possess dominate, 144
possess presence, 20 possess dementation, 25 possess chimerstry, 27 possess
vicissitude. Again, i shouldn't invoke numbers : obfuscate has "spying
mission". Does it count as a normal bleed modifier ?
Basically, almost all vampires can play +1 Bleed after bleeding. You can
also toss some Sabbat inquisitor, Laptops and Legendary vampires if you
really need those bleed bonuses. Also note that bleeding is strong when
paired with the correct discipline : Obfuscate, obtenebration... Celerity
bleed will not help you. We might say that Bleed is a powerful tactics if
you dedicate your deck to bleeding. Same thing for combat.

> - combat needs to be more efficient. It is the most varied tactic in VtES,
> yet it remains the less effective.

combat is efficient. combat can shutdown an entire deck, no matter what the
concept, no matter what the cards. In the hand of skilled players, well buit
combat decks kill non-combat decks. No need to change this aspect of the
game only because some people use numbers to measure things that cannot be
measured by numbers.

hey ! nothing personnal =) just my two corruption counters !
reyda

On Fri, 6 Jul 2001 15:18:02 +0100, "Flux" <fl...@netc.pt> wrote:

>Hello everyone.
>
>I've been thinking about the whole combat/S:CE situation lately, and one
>argument for S:CE sort of stuck out among the rest: that combat is just a
>tactic, and therefore should not be allowed to dominate VtES strategies. I
>believe LSJ himself has invoked this principle a few times, and certainly
>the recent new cards seem to bear this out.

Well, it's not so much an argument for S:CE as it is an argument
against tipping the balance by changing -that- mechanic.

The basic strategy of the game: reduce your prey's pool to zero.

Everything about the game should be, in some fashion, related to that
strategy, and the cards that will see the most use will be the ones
most closely related.

>Of course, us combat fans counter that combat should be an important part of
>the game, and point to (among other things) the complexity of combat and the
>large amount of rules attached to it, but complexity does not mean it should
>rule the game, not even that it is an important part of it.

Us combat fans have also long ago done the analysis you did below, so
don't be surprised when I skim over it lightly. ;)

>However, there is one thing that should be a reasonable indication of how
>important this mechanic should be to the game: the number of cards dedicated
>to this tactic, and the potential number of decks that can use it.

...and the number of cards that can be PLAYED, related to the mechanic
itself. More below.

>So, let's see the numbers:
>
>By card type:
>-Action 147
>-Action Modifier 63+9+2
>-Ally 50
>-Combat 177+9+2
>-Equipment 71
>-Master 248
>-Political 109
>-Reaction 59+2+2
>-Retainer 29
>
>It's pretty clear that combat is the dominant minion card type. Only Master

Somewhat misleading. "Actions" are right behind them, at 147. And
you can only play one action card per action, while you can play
multiple cards per combat.

This indicates that there is a significantly greater amount of variety
in the actions themselves, ... which is a good thing! There is only
so much variety in bleed. The mechanic is "reduce prey's pool", and
the only variety after that comes from "how much". The side effects,
such as Propaganda, are amusing, but you notice that Propaganda
doesn't hit the table very often? The primary concern is the -amount-
of the bleed. =)

>But let's look at discipline distribution then:
>
>Crypt Stats by discipline:

(snipped)

Tabdamaged, unfortunately =/ This doesn't line up properly in either
variable- or fixed-width fonts.

>Wow! Combat _is_ quite abundant. Many disciplines are almost exclusively
>dedicated to combat, and the number of discipline points dedicated to
>combat-worthy disciplines is more than double the number dedicated to any
>other tactic! That is, potentially, a lot more vampires can inflict

>both of these are still far from those of combat or even bleed. This also
>explains why so many players think that combat is exciting, and bleeding is
>boring: there is a lot more potential variety for combat than for bleeding.

Correct. But this isn't due to numbers of cards -- this is simply
because bleeding is a purely-numerical strategy. Combat has cards
which touch upon many more facets of the game than bleeding does
(witness Fleshcraft; the strike for 1 damage is almost totally
irrelevant to the usefulness of the card).

>I already stated my positions in relation to S:CE and combat in general in
>other recent posts, so I'll spare you from reading them again here, though I
>will point a couple of things that should be obvious based on this evidence:

Hmmmmm... I dunno. :)

>- we need more bleed disciplines. In fact, we need more variety for all of
>the base tactics. Some things have improved (intercept, for example), but
>largely all has remained the same since Jyhad.

I disagree. There is plenty of bleed in the game right now, and as I
mentioned above, all you can do with bleed is... well... bleed.
Tacking on a +2 bleed card to Animalism, for example, provides
variety, but does it actually improve the game? It gives the Gangrel
easy bruise-and-bleed ability, right? Or does it just further
marginalize combat as the Nosferatu begin to run wild with the new
stealth-bleed creation?

>- combat needs to be more efficient. It is the most varied tactic in VtES,
>yet it remains the less effective.

Except that it does almost nothing to further the basic idea of the
game, which is "reduce prey's pool". If you torporize ALL your prey's
minions, they must spend pool to bring more out; but pure-combat
decks, in general, do not actually have a problem torporizing a bunch
of their prey's minions. The problem comes in when they are unable to
defend against their predator AS WELL as hose down their prey.
Potence Rush decks can often manage both, but this is a direct
testament to both the effectiveness of Potence as a combat discipline,
and to the number of distinct small vampires with pot/POT available.
Comparing Potence to some other disciplines, we find some interesting
numbers as well. (I'm ignoring Quietus deliberately, as FN hasn't
shaken itself out completely yet.)

POTENCE: found on 144 out of 423 vampires, or 34%.
PROTEAN: found on 61 out of 423, or 14%.
CELERITY: found on 149 out of 423: 34% again.
FORTITUDE: found on 121 out of 423: 29%.
THAUMATURGY: found on 70 out of 423: 15%.

...Moving on and splitting down the disciplines into "type" of cards:

POTENCE has 1 action card and 21 combat cards.
PROTEAN has 3 actions, 3 action modifiers, 1 "combo" (Rapid Change),
15 combat cards, and 1 retainer.
CELERITY has 3 actions, 1 action modifier, and 18 combat cards.
FORTITUDE has 6 actions, 5 action modifiers, and 11 combat cards.
THAUMATURGY has 4 actions, 1 action modifier, 1 retainer, and 15
combat cards.

...So really, only Potence and Celerity are TRULY pure-combat
disciplines. Breaking it down even further for each:

POTENCE only has four combat cards that are not either (a) damaging
strikes, or (b) direct support for damaging strikes (Torn Signpost,
IG). Fractured Armament and Shattering Blow are equipment-related.
Relentless Pursuit is a press. And Disarm isn't "damage" in and of
itself; you have to have done damage in some other way. This makes 17
cards that all read, in some form or other, "I hit you."

What this means is that almost the ENTIRE discipline of Potence is
designed around one thing: hitting people for lots. This makes for a
very effective mono-discipline deck, even if Immortal Grapple were NOT
included! Don't believe me? Get all the POT weenies, include a bunch
of Increased Strengths, Thrown Gates, and POT skill cards. Season
with Computer Hacking, Blood Dolls, Wakes, and intercept locations to
taste. Mix well and serve.

PROTEAN, by comparison, has only 7 "damaging" combat cards. It has 4
maneuver/press cards, 2 prevent cards, and 3 S:CE cards(!). It makes
an excellent discipline in its own right, but is it so surprising
anymore that pure-Protean combat has its troubles?

CELERITY is really a combat -support- discipline, as the vast majority
of its cards are either maneuvers, presses, or additional strikes.
There are also not a few cards in there whose purpose is actually
-defensive- (Dodge, S:CE).

FORTITUDE is much more focused, which should come as no surprise since
it IS one of the premier ways to defeat combat; all 11 of its combat
cards read "prevent X damage", again in varying flavors.

THAUMATURGY comes with its own problems; many of its combat cards have
heavy restrictions on them. Number of first-round damaging combat
cards: 8. Number of SECOND-round damaging combat cards: 5. And
there are 2 utility maneuver/press cards in there, as well. No wonder
the Tremere were screwed - it's hard enough just to get to a second
round with them, much less get all the cards you need to make them
kill things... and that's without even including S:CE in the picture.

...So as it turns out, the discipline that is best held up as a
"counter" to S:CE also turns out to be the overall best combat
discipline anyway. Is this indicating a problem with S:CE, or a
problem with people's approach to combat? From what I can see, combat
seems to have been designed as an ADJUNCT to bleeding or voting;
something that should be a part of everyone's deck, but not their
primary strategy. If it was intended to be a primary strategy, I
think Protean and Thaumaturgy might look a bit different.

Are people approaching combat wrong? Yeah, I think so. But I've made
this one long enough - a bit more later. (gotta swap laundry!)

-- Derek

enough.

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Alternatively, the fact that combat enables more card-playing
opportunities could easily be seen as the reason that there are more
"combat" cards than other "icons".

One could alternatively look at "cards played during the resolution of
an action (incl. combat)" vs. "cards played before the resolution of
an action".

Or break it down into "strike cards", "press cards", etc.

Or explain it by the fact that combat is a varied affair whereas
bleeding, for example, permits fewer variations on the theme. This
could even be seen as combat's purpose - to break up the "routine"
that is the rest of the game.

Or spin the numbers in many other ways.
